etymology: From the Greek Patrobas, a shortened form meaning “life of his father” or “paternal,” likely a contraction of Patrobios.
biblical_def: Patrobas is one of the believers at Rome whom the apostle Paul singles out for greeting in the closing chapter of his great epistle, named in a cluster of five: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them” (Rom 16:14). Of his life, his trade, his trials, and his death the Word tells us nothing further; he is a name and no more. Yet that very obscurity preaches. The Holy Spirit, who omitted whole reigns of kings in a sentence, took care to set down Patrobas by name in the imperishable record of Scripture. He was known and loved by Paul, and known and chosen of God before the foundation of the world. The grouping “and the brethren which are with them” suggests Patrobas belonged to a household or house-fellowship of saints, the ordinary soil in which the early church grew. Tradition counts him among the seventy and makes him a martyr, but Scripture is silent, and where Scripture is silent we hold our peace. What we may say with certainty is that his name is written in heaven (Luk 10:20), which is honor enough. The roll of Romans 16 is a standing rebuke to every notion that only the prominent matter to God; the Head of the church numbers His least members and forgets none of them.
webster_summary: A Christian at Rome greeted by Paul in Romans 16, of whom nothing else is recorded in Scripture.

corruption_summary: The honour of the obscure saint, remembered by name in heaven though forgotten on earth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Patrobas is the dignity God assigns to His unknown people. A single name in a list of greetings, he stands for the thousands of faithful who never preach, never write, never lead, and yet are precious to Christ and inscribed in the Lamb’s book of life.

Our age measures worth by visibility and platform; the Spirit measures it by union with Christ. Patrobas rebukes the hunger for recognition that gnaws even at believers. To be known by God is infinitely more than to be known by men, and the saint who labours in obscurity loses nothing, for the Judge of all the earth keeps a perfect record and will not forget the work and labour of love shown toward His name.

etymology: A Greek name borrowed from Nereus, a sea-deity of pagan myth, here borne by a Roman believer with no taint of its origin.
biblical_def: Nereus is a saint of the Roman church greeted by Paul together with his sister: “Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them” (Rom 16:15). His sister, unnamed, is honoured alongside him, a quiet testimony that brother and sister together had owned the Lord Jesus. Scripture tells us nothing more of either, yet the bare notice carries weight. That a household should be found in Christ, kin bound not only by blood but by the new birth, is one of grace’s sweetest fruits. The name Nereus was Greek and, in its origin, the name of a sea-god of the heathen; that a man so named should appear among the saints of Rome shows how the gospel reaches into pagan soil and claims its own. Tradition associates Nereus with the household of a noble Roman lady and counts him a martyr, but the inspired record is silent and we add nothing to it. The final clause, “and all the saints which are with them,” gathers Nereus into a fellowship of believers, again the house-church pattern of the early faith. He is remembered for one thing only: he belonged to Christ and to Christ’s people, and that is the whole sum of a man’s blessedness.

corruption_summary: The grace of a believing household, brother and sister bound together in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Nereus is the blessing of kindred in the faith. A brother and a sister, both saved, both saluted, show how the gospel claims whole families and binds natural ties with the stronger bond of the new birth.

We ought to pray and labour that our own households, like that of Nereus, may be found wholly in Christ. The Lord delights to gather families to Himself, and the sister honoured at her brother’s side reminds us that the meanest and most anonymous believer shares fully in the salvation that is in Christ Jesus.

etymology: A Greek name, likely a contraction of Olympiodorus, “gift of Olympus,” the mountain reckoned the seat of the heathen gods.
biblical_def: Olympas is the last of the named believers in Paul’s roll of greetings to the Roman church: “Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them” (Rom 16:15). Like several about him, his name is Greek and bears, in its origin, the mark of pagan religion, being drawn from Olympus, the fabled dwelling of the false gods. That such a man should stand among the saints of Rome is itself a sermon on the reach of sovereign grace, which calls men out of darkness and gives them a new and better citizenship in heaven. Scripture says nothing else of Olympas; no deed, no word, no death is recorded. He is gathered with “all the saints which are with them,” one more member of a house-fellowship in the great city. Tradition, as with his companions, supplies a martyr’s end, but the inspired page is silent and we will not go beyond it. The lesson is plain and weighty: the Lord knows them that are His, and not one of His own, however nameless to the world and however briefly noted in His Word, is lost or forgotten. Olympas is honoured forever by a single mention from the pen of the apostle, moved by the Holy Ghost.
webster_summary: A Christian at Rome, last named in Paul’s greetings, of whom nothing else is recorded.

corruption_summary: The reach of grace that calls men out of paganism into the household of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Olympas is the sovereign reach of the gospel. A man whose very name pointed to the throne of false gods is found among the saints, his citizenship now in heaven and his name on the apostle’s lips.

We learn that no soil is too pagan for grace to claim its own. The Lord gathers His elect from every people and every former darkness, and He keeps a perfect roll of them. Olympas, last and least in the human record, is fully and forever the Lord’s, for the Lord knoweth them that are His.

etymology: A Greek name, a contracted form (as of Hermodorus or Hermogenes), bearing the element Hermes, the name of a pagan messenger-god.
biblical_def: Hermas is a believer of the Roman church greeted by Paul: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them” (Rom 16:14). He is named in a group of five men, set just before another saint called Hermes, both names sharing the same pagan root yet borne now by men in Christ. Of this Hermas the inspired record tells us nothing beyond the greeting; his labours and his end are unknown to us. An ancient tradition has sought to identify this Hermas with the author of the second-century work “The Shepherd of Hermas,” and Origen and others entertained the link; but this rests on no solid ground, the dates strain against it, and we ought not build doctrine or biography upon a guess. The Hermas of this entry is simply the disciple at Rome whom Paul loved and saluted, one of the “brethren which are with them” in a household of the faith. His worth lies not in any deed history records but in his union with Christ. The Spirit set his name in Scripture, and that is honour beyond the reach of fame. Like his fellows in this list, he stands for the great company of ordinary saints whom God numbers, names, and keeps to the end.
webster_summary: A Christian at Rome greeted by Paul in Romans 16; not to be confidently identified with the later writer of “The Shepherd.”

corruption_summary: The danger of building biography on tradition rather than the sober witness of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Hermas is restraint where Scripture is silent. The hasty identification of this man with the author of “The Shepherd” warns us not to dress a bare name in a borrowed history; we honour the Word by holding to what it says and no more.

His honour, like that of his fellows, lies wholly in being known to Christ. The disciple at Rome teaches us that fame is nothing and union with the Saviour is everything. The Lord will not blot out the name of him that overcometh, and that promise covers every obscure saint whom the world never knew.

etymology: A Greek name, a contracted form (as of Nymphodorus) bearing the element nymphe, “bride” or “nymph.”
biblical_def: Nymphas is a believer at or near Laodicea in whose house a congregation of the saints met, greeted by Paul in the close of Colossians: “Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house” (Col 4:15). Here we see the early church in its native form, gathered not in grand buildings but in the homes of its members, where a godly host opened his doors that the body of Christ might assemble for the Word, prayer, and the breaking of bread. Such house-churches dot the New Testament: that of Aquila and Priscilla (Rom 16:5), that in the house of Philemon (Phm 2), and this of Nymphas. To host the church was a costly and honourable service, exposing the household to expense and, in days of persecution, to danger. Nymphas stands therefore as a pattern of hospitality used for the gospel, of a Christian home set apart to the worship of God. Of the man himself we know nothing further. His house at Laodicea sat near a church the risen Christ would soon rebuke for lukewarmness (Rev 3:14–19), a sobering nearness. Yet Nymphas himself is named with honour, a saint whose dwelling became a sanctuary, and whose ordinary house was made holy by the assembling of the people of God within it.
webster_summary: A believer of the Laodicean region in whose house a church assembled, greeted by Paul in Colossians.

corruption_summary: The honourable service of hospitality, the Christian home opened for the worship of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Nymphas is the dignity of the house-church and of hospitality spent upon the gospel. A man opened his home, and it became a place where Christ was worshipped and His people gathered.

Our age prizes private comfort and guards the home against intrusion; Nymphas teaches the opposite, a dwelling held loosely and offered freely to the saints. The church does not depend upon costly buildings but upon believing households and the assembling of the people of God. To host the church is no small thing, but a service the Lord honours and Scripture records.

etymology: From the Hebrew Qenaz, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “hunter” or “possession,” giving rise to the gentilic “Kenizzite.”
biblical_def: Kenaz is a name borne by more than one man in the Scriptures, and from it springs the family-line called Kenizzite. First, Kenaz appears among the descendants of Esau, a duke of Edom: “the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz” (Gen 36:11), and he is again listed as a duke (Gen 36:15). Second, and chiefly in the line of Israel, Kenaz is reckoned the father of Othniel, the first of the judges, and the younger brother of Caleb: “And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took it” (Jdg 1:13; compare Jos 15:17). Othniel won Achsah, Caleb’s daughter, by taking Kirjath-sepher, and later delivered Israel from Chushan-rishathaim. Kenaz appears yet again in the genealogy of Judah: “And the sons of Othniel; Hathath, and Meonothai… and the sons of Elah, even Kenaz” (1Ch 4:13–15). The Kenizzites were a people Abraham was told would be dispossessed when the seed inherited the land (Gen 15:19), yet Caleb is repeatedly called “the Kenizzite” (Num 32:12; Jos 14:6), which shows how grace grafted this stock into Judah and made of it some of Israel’s most faithful men. From a line marked for dispossession came Caleb who wholly followed the Lord and Othniel who judged Israel in righteousness, a standing proof that the mercy of God overrides the disabilities of birth.
webster_summary: A Hebrew name borne by a duke of Edom and by the father of Othniel; source of the family-name Kenizzite.

corruption_summary: The grace of God grafting a dispossessed stock into Judah and raising up faithful men from it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Kenaz and the Kenizzites is the sovereign mercy that overrides birth. From a line named among the peoples to be dispossessed came Caleb, who wholly followed the Lord, and Othniel, the first judge of Israel.

Grace is no respecter of pedigree. The Kenizzite was reckoned with Judah, and his sons stood among the most faithful of the nation. So the gospel takes those who were strangers and aliens and makes them fellow-citizens with the saints, that no man may boast in his lineage but only in the God who calls and grafts in whom He will.

etymology: From the Greek Epainetos, “praised” or “worthy of praise,” from epaineo, to commend.
biblical_def: Epaenetus is a believer at Rome whom the apostle Paul greets with peculiar warmth: “Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ” (Rom 16:5). Two marks of honour rest upon him. First, he was Paul’s wellbeloved, a man dear to the apostle’s heart, knit to him in the bond of the gospel. Second, and greater, he was “the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ,” among the earliest in that region to be brought from darkness to light and laid as a first sheaf upon the altar of God. The figure is drawn from the law, where the firstfruits of the harvest were offered to the Lord as a pledge of the whole crop to follow (Lev 23:10). So Epaenetus, an early convert, was a token and earnest of the great harvest the gospel would reap. Of his after-life Scripture tells us nothing; he is a name, a love, and a firstfruit, and no more. Yet that is enough. The Spirit set down his name forever as one whom Christ claimed early and Paul loved dearly. He stands for every believer who, brought first out of a household or a region, becomes a pledge that God has more people there, and a standing encouragement to labour on where one soul has already been won.

The firstfruit teaches patience and hope to those who labour for souls. One conversion is no small thing; it is an earnest of more, a token that the Lord is at work in a place. Epaenetus, Paul’s wellbeloved, reminds us that the Saviour claims men one by one, and that the first to come stands as a promise of the multitude that shall follow.

etymology: From the Hebrew, “portion of the sun” or “extra portion”; also called Timnath-heres, “portion of the sun,” the elements transposed.
biblical_def: Timnath-serah was the city in the hill country of Ephraim granted to Joshua the son of Nun for his inheritance, and the place where he was buried. When the dividing of the land was finished, “the children of Israel gave an inheritance to Joshua the son of Nun among them: according to the word of the LORD they gave him the city which he asked, even Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim: and he built the city, and dwelt therein” (Jos 19:50). It is fitting that the great captain who led Israel into Canaan and apportioned every tribe its lot received his own portion last and at his own asking, a single city which he himself built. There he was laid to rest: “And they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-serah, which is in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash” (Jos 24:30). The same place is named Timnath-heres in the book of Judges, the two elements of the name transposed: “they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-heres, in the mount of Ephraim” (Jdg 2:9). The modest inheritance of so great a servant rebukes all grasping ambition. Joshua, who could have claimed much, asked for one city, built it, dwelt in it, and there laid down his bones beside the people he had served. His grave in Ephraim stands as a monument to a life wholly given to the Lord and to His covenant promises.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Timnath-serah is contentment and self-forgetful service. Joshua divided a whole land to others and took for himself a single city, which he built with his own hand and where he was laid to rest.

The great captain’s humble inheritance rebukes every grasping spirit. He who could have seized much asked little, served the Lord wholly to the end, and left behind no monument but a grave in Ephraim and a people brought into their inheritance. So the faithful servant looks not for reward in this life, but for the city whose builder and maker is God.

etymology: From the Hebrew, “lofty” or “exalted,” from a root meaning to be high, fitting a fortified hill-town.
biblical_def: Jogbehah was a fortified town east of the Jordan, built by the children of Gad among the cities they raised in the cattle-country of Gilead. When Reuben and Gad received their inheritance beyond Jordan, “the children of Gad built Dibon, and Ataroth, and Aroer, and Atroth, Shophan, and Jaazer, and Jogbehah” (Num 32:34–35). These were strong places, walled for defence and provided with folds for their flocks, the settled possession of tribes given to husbandry on the eastern frontier. Jogbehah appears once more in the days of Gideon, on the route of his famous pursuit of the kings of Midian. Having routed the great host with three hundred men, Gideon pressed after the fleeing princes Zebah and Zalmunna: “And Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and smote the host: for the host was secure” (Jdg 8:11). Coming upon them by the desert track, where they thought themselves safe, he fell upon the camp and completed the deliverance of Israel. Thus this small Transjordan town, built by Gad, became a landmark in one of the great victories of faith, when the Lord saved Israel by a handful that the glory might be His alone. Jogbehah stands as a quiet witness to the providence that marks even the obscure places by which His salvation is wrought.
webster_summary: A fortified town east of Jordan built by the tribe of Gad, on the route of Gideon’s pursuit of Midian.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Jogbehah is the care of God over the least places of His purpose. A small town built by Gad becomes a landmark in Gideon’s victory, where the Lord saved Israel by three hundred men that no flesh might glory.

The obscure things of the field are not forgotten in the record of redemption. Jogbehah teaches that the Lord works His salvation through ordinary places and small means, overthrowing the proud host by the weak, that the praise might rest wholly upon Him who gives the victory.

etymology: From the Latin Rufus, “red” or “red-haired,” a very common name among the Romans.
biblical_def: Rufus is a believer at Rome greeted by Paul with a singular tenderness: “Salute Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine” (Rom 16:13). Two things are said of him. He is “chosen in the Lord,” a phrase that lifts the veil upon the doctrine of election, marking Rufus as one of those whom God set His love upon and chose in Christ before the foundation of the world. And his mother had been as a mother to Paul; the apostle, who counted himself debtor to no earthly comfort, gratefully owns that this woman had shown him a mother’s kindness, and so calls her “his mother and mine.” An ancient and not unlikely tradition identifies this Rufus with the Rufus named by Mark, son of Simon the Cyrenian who bore the cross of Christ: “the father of Alexander and Rufus” (Mar 15:21). Mark, writing (as held) for the Roman church, names the sons as men known to his readers, which fits a Rufus dwelling at Rome. If so, the son of the cross-bearer became a chosen vessel, and the household that touched the Saviour’s passion was gathered into His church. Yet Scripture does not press the link, and neither will we. What is certain is enough: Rufus was chosen in the Lord, and his mother was a mother in Israel whose kindness the great apostle did not forget.

corruption_summary: A saint marked “chosen in the Lord,” and the honoured kindness of a mother in Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Rufus is the sweetness of electing grace brought down to a single named man. To be “chosen in the Lord” is the ground of all a believer’s blessedness, and Paul greets Rufus by that very title.

The greeting honours also a mother’s love. She who mothered Paul stands for the unnumbered women whose quiet kindness sustains the servants of Christ. The household perhaps touched by the cross-bearing of Simon was gathered into the church; and whether or not the link holds, the certainty remains, that God chooses His own and binds them in families of faith and labours of love.
